content.heading: 8.6 Curves and Surfaces
content.paragraph: For thousands of years, builders used long thin strips of wood to create the hull of a boat. In more recent times, designers used long, flexible metal strips to lay out the surfaces of cars and airplanes. Weights and pegs shaped the strips into smooth curves called natural cubic splines. The curve between two successive control points (pegs or weights) has a parametric representation using cubic polynomials. Unfortunately, such curves have the property that moving one control point affects the shape of the entire curve, because of physical forces that the pegs and weights exert on the strip. Design engineers had long wanted local control of the curve—in which movement of one control point would affect only a small portion of the curve. In 1962, a French automotive engineer, Pierre Bézier, solved this problem by adding extra control points and using a class of curves now called by his name.
content.heading: Bézier Curves
content.paragraph: The curves described in this section play an important role in computer graphics as well as engineering. For example, they are used in Adobe Illustrator and Macromedia Freehand, and in application programming languages such as OpenGL. These curves permit a program to store exact information about curved segments and surfaces in a relatively small number of control points. All graphics commands for the segments and surfaces have only to be computed for the control points. The special structure of these curves also speeds up other calculations in the “graphics pipeline” that creates the final display on the viewing screen.

Exercises in Section 8.3 introduced quadratic Bézier curves and showed one method for constructing Bézier curves of higher degree. The discussion here focuses on quadratic and cubic Bézier curves, which are determined by three or four control points, denoted by $\textbf{p}_{0}$, $\textbf{p}_{1}$, $\textbf{p}_{2}$, and $\textbf{p}_{3}$. These points can be in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ or $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, or they can be represented by homogeneous forms in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ or $\text{ℝ}^{4}$. The standard parametric descriptions of these curves, for $0 \leq t \leq 1$, are

Figure1 shows two typical curves. Usually, the curves pass through only the initial and terminal control points, but a Bézier curve is always in the convex hull of its control points. (See Exercises 25–28 in Section 8.3.)

image.alt: Quadratic and cubic Bezier curves with three and four control points, respectively, are shown.

content.paragraph: Bézier curves are useful in computer graphics because their essential properties are preserved under the action of linear transformations and translations. The curves in Figure 1 suggest that the control points determine the tangent lines to the curves at the initial and terminal control points. Recall from calculus that for any parametric curve, say $\textbf{y}(t)$, the direction of the tangent line to the curve at a point $\textbf{y}(t)$ is given by the derivative $\mathbf{y}\prime(t)$, called the tangent vector of the curve. (This derivative is computed entry by entry.)

content.heading: Connecting Two Bézier Curves
content.paragraph: Two basic Bézier curves can be joined end to end, with the terminal point of the first curve $\textbf{x}(t)$ being the initial point $\textbf{p}_{2}$ of the second curve $\textbf{y}(t)$. The combined curve is said to have $G^{0}$ geometric continuity (at $\textbf{p}_{2}$) because the two segments join at $\textbf{p}_{2}$. If the tangent line to curve $1$ at $\textbf{p}_{2}$ has a different direction than the tangent line to curve $2$, then a “corner,” or abrupt change of direction, may be apparent at $\textbf{p}_{2}$. See Figure 2.

image.alt: A figure shows G to the 0 continuity with four line segments in the form a step along with two Bezier curves.

content.paragraph: To avoid a sharp bend, it usually suffices to adjust the curves to have what is called $G^{1}$ geometric continuity, where both tangent vectors at $\textbf{p}_{2}$ point in the same direction. That is, the derivatives $\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$ and $\mathbf{y}\prime(0)$ point in the same direction, even though their magnitudes may be different. When the tangent vectors are actually equal at $\textbf{p}_{2}$, the tangent vector is continuous at $\textbf{p}_{2}$, and the combined curve is said to have $C^{1}$ continuity, or $C^{1}$ parametric continuity. Figure 3 shows $G^{1}$ continuity in (a) and $C^{1}$ continuity in (b).

image.alt: A graph shows G to the continuity and C to the 1 continuity with four control points in the form of a rectangle with its bottom left open.

content.paragraph: Two curves have $C^{2}$ (parametric) continuity when they have $C^{1}$ continuity and the second derivatives $\mathbf{x}''(1)$ and $\mathbf{y}''(0)$ are equal. This is possible for cubic Bézier curves, but it severely limits the positions of the control points. Another class of cubic curves, called $B\text{-}splines$, always have $C^{2}$ continuity because each pair of curves share three control points rather than one. Graphics figures using $\text{B-splines}$ have more control points and consequently require more computations. Some exercises for this section examine these curves.

Surprisingly, if $\textbf{x}(t)$ and $\textbf{y}(t)$ join at $\textbf{p}_{3}$, the apparent smoothness of the curve at $\textbf{p}_{3}$ is usually the same for both $G^{1}$ continuity and $C^{1}$ continuity. This is because the magnitude of $\mathbf{x}\prime(t)$ is not related to the physical shape of the curve. The magnitude reflects only the mathematical parameterization of the curve. For instance, if a new vector function $\textbf{z}(t)$ equals $\textbf{x}(2t)$, then the point $\textbf{z}(t)$ traverses the curve from $\textbf{p}_{0}$ to $\textbf{p}_{3}$ twice as fast as the original version, because $2t$ reaches $1$ when $t$ is $.5$. But, by the chain rule of calculus, $\mathbf{z}\prime(t) = 2 \cdot \mathbf{x}\prime(2t)$, so the tangent vector to $\textbf{z}(t)$ at $\textbf{p}_{3}$ is twice the tangent vector to $\textbf{x}(t)$ at $\textbf{p}_{3}$.﻿

In practice, many simple Bézier curves are joined to create graphics objects. Typesetting programs provide one important application, because many letters in a type font involve curved segments. Each letter in a PostScript® font, for example, is stored as a set of control points, along with information on how to construct the “outline” of the letter using line segments and Bézier curves. Enlarging such a letter basically requires multiplying the coordinates of each control point by one constant scale factor. Once the outline of the letter has been computed, the appropriate solid parts of the letter are filled in. Figure5 illustrates this for a character in a PostScript font. Note the control points.

image.alt: Two figures show a PostScript character Q along with its control points given by line segments.

Other parametric cubic curves in computer graphics are written in this form, too. For instance, if the entries in the matrix $M_{B}$ are changed appropriately, the resulting curves are $\text{B-splines}$. They are “smoother” than Bézier curves, but they do not pass through any of the control points. A Hermite cubic curve arises when the matrix $M_{B}$ is replaced by a Hermite basis matrix. In this case, the columns of the geometry matrix consist of the starting and ending points of the curves and the tangent vectors to the curves at those points.1
The Bézier curve in equation (4) can also be “factored” in another way, to be used in the discussion of Bézier surfaces. For convenience later, the parameter $t$ is replaced by a parameter $s$:

The matrix of control points in (5) is called a geometry vector. This should be viewed as a $4 \times 1$ block (partitioned) matrix whose entries are column vectors. content.heading: Approximations to Curves and Surfaces
content.paragraph: In CAD programs and in programs used to create realistic computer games, the designer often works at a graphics workstation to compose a “scene” involving various geometric structures. This process requires interaction between the designer and the geometric objects. Each slight repositioning of an object requires new mathematical computations by the graphics program. Bézier curves and surfaces can be useful in this process because they involve fewer control points than objects approximated by many polygons. This dramatically reduces the computation time and speeds up the designer’s work.

After the scene composition, however, the final image preparation has different computational demands that are more easily met by objects consisting of flat surfaces and straight edges, such as polyhedra. The designer needs to render the scene, by introducing light sources, adding color and texture to surfaces, and simulating reflections from the surfaces.

Computing the direction of a reflected light at a point $\textbf{p}$ on a surface, for instance, requires knowing the directions of both the incoming light and the surface normal—the vector perpendicular to the tangent plane at $\textbf{p}$. Computing such normal vectors is much easier on a surface composed of, say, tiny flat polygons than on a curved surface whose normal vector changes continuously as $\textbf{p}$ moves. If $\textbf{p}_{1}$, $\textbf{p}_{2}$, and $\textbf{p}_{3}$ are adjacent vertices of a flat polygon, then the surface normal is just plus or minus the cross product $\left( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1} \right) \times \left( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{3} \right)$. When the polygon is small, only one normal vector is needed for rendering the entire polygon. Also, two widely used shading routines, Gouraud shading and Phong shading, both require a surface to be defined by polygons.

As a result of these needs for flat surfaces, the Bézier curves and surfaces from the scene composition stage now are usually approximated by straight line segments and polyhedral surfaces. The basic idea for approximating a Bézier curve or surface is to divide the curve or surface into smaller pieces, with more and more control points.
content.heading: Recursive Subdivision of Bézier Curves and Surfaces
content.paragraph: Figure 7 shows the four control points $\textbf{p}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{p}_{3}$ for a Bézier curve, along with control points for two new curves, each coinciding with half of the original curve. The “left” curve begins at $\textbf{q}_{0} = \textbf{p}_{0}$ and ends at $\textbf{q}_{3}$, at the midpoint of the original curve. The “right” curve begins at $\textbf{r}_{0} = \textbf{q}_{3}$ and ends at $\textbf{r}_{3} = \textbf{p}_{3}$.﻿

image.alt: A figure shows the Bezier curve along with its subdivision inside an isosceles trapezium that is left open at the bottom.

content.paragraph: Figure8 shows how the new control points enclose regions that are “thinner” than the region enclosed by the original control points. As the distances between the control points decrease, the control points of each curve segment also move closer to a line segment. This variation-diminishing property of Bézier curves depends on the fact that a Bézier curve always lies in the convex hull of the control points.

figure.caption: Convex hulls of the control points

image.alt: A figure shows the convex hulls of the control points with a Bezier curve, a subdivision of the Bezier curve, and a triangle intersecting at a point inside an isosceles trapezium.

content.paragraph: This completes one step of the subdivision process. The “recursion” begins, and both new curves are subdivided. The recursion continues to a depth at which all curves are sufficiently straight. Alternatively, at each step the recursion can be “adaptive” and not subdivide one of the two new curves if that curve is sufficiently straight. Once the subdivision completely stops, the endpoints of each curve are joined by line segments, and the scene is ready for the next step in the final image preparation.

A Bézier bicubic surface has the same variation-diminishing property as the Bézier curves that make up each cross-section of the surface, so the process described above can be applied in each cross-section. With the details omitted, here is the basic strategy. Consider the four “parallel” Bézier curves whose parameter is $s$, and apply the subdivision process to each of them. This produces four sets of eight control points; each set determines a curve as $s$ varies from $0$ to $1$. As $t$ varies, however, there are eight curves, each with four control points. Apply the subdivision process to each of these sets of four points, creating a total of $64$ control points. Adaptive recursion is possible in this setting, too, but there are some subtleties involved.2

TrueType® fonts, created by Apple Computer and Adobe Systems, use quadratic Bézier curves, while PostScript® fonts, created by Microsoft, use cubic Bézier curves. The cubic curves provide more flexibility for typeface design, but it is important to Microsoft that every typeface using quadratic curves can be transformed into one that uses cubic curves. Suppose that $\textbf{w}(t)$ is a quadratic curve, with control points $\textbf{p}_{0}$, $\textbf{p}_{1}$, and $\textbf{p}_{2}$.﻿
